[Migrating from Testing Library | Playwright](https://playwright.dev/docs/testing-library)\n\n# Playwright Component Testing for React\n\nPlaywright offers experimental component testing capabilities for React applications.[1][3] Here's what you need to know:\n\n## Getting Started\n\nInstallation is straightforward using the command:[1][3]\n&#96;&#96;&#96;bash\nnpm init playwright@latest -- --ct\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nThis creates necessary configuration files including a &#96;playwright/index.html&#96; file (with a root div for mounting components) and test files.[1][3]\n\n## Basic Test Structure\n\nA typical component test looks like this:[1][3]\n&#96;&#96;&#96;js\nimport { test, expect } from '@playwright/experimental-ct-react';\nimport App from './App';\n\ntest('should work', async ({ mount }) =\u003e {\n  const component = await mount(\u003cApp /\u003e);\n  await expect(component).toContainText('Learn React');\n});\n&#96;&#96;&#96;\n\nRun tests with &#96;npm run test-ct&#96;.[1][3]\n\n## Key Advantages\n\nTests run in Node.js while components run in a real browser, combining the benefits of both environments.[1][3] This enables real clicks, actual layout execution, and visual regression testing while leveraging Node.js capabilities and Playwright features like parallel testing and tracing.[1][3]\n\n## Important Limitations\n\n- You can only pass plain JavaScript objects and built-in types (strings, numbers, dates) to components—not complex Node.js objects[1][3]\n- You cannot pass data synchronously through callbacks, as the callback lives in Node while the component runs in the browser[1][3]\n\n## Migration from Testing Library\n\nPlaywright provides migration guidance from React Testing Library, with equivalent APIs (e.g., &#96;render()&#96; → &#96;mount()&#96;, &#96;screen&#96; → &#96;component&#96;).[4][5]",

## Bottom Line
For your current repo, most of this list falls into 3 buckets:

- Keep using what already matches your stack: `Next.js`, `TypeScript`, `Tailwind`, `Drizzle`, `ESLint`, `Vitest`, `Playwright`, `pnpm`, `PostCSS`, `tsx`, `Node.js`, `SWC`.
- Add a small number of high-value tools soon: `Knip`, `CSpell`, `MSW`, `Sentry`, `size-limit`, and maybe `SVGO`/`SVGR`.
- Skip the rest unless your roadmap changes, because many are competing frameworks, alternate bundlers, alternate ORMs, or release/monorepo tooling you do not need for a single Next.js 16 app with its own CMS.

## Best Candidates For Your Project
If I had to shortlist the most useful additions for this specific repo, I’d pick these:

- `Knip`: best cleanup tool for unused files, exports, and dependencies.
- `CSpell`: catches bad spelling in UI text, docs, and code identifiers with very low maintenance cost.
- `Mock Service Worker`: best next testing upgrade for realistic API mocking in `Vitest` and `Playwright`.
- `Sentry`: best production monitoring upgrade once the site/admin are live.
- `size-limit`: very relevant for a public portfolio where bundle weight matters.
- `SVGO`: useful if you keep raw SVG assets.
- `SVGR`: useful if you often turn SVGs into React components.
- `simple-git-hooks` or `husky` + `lint-staged` + `commitlint`: worth it if you want stricter repo hygiene.
- `next-intl`: only if you plan multilingual content.
- `MDX` / `Next.js MDX` / `Remark`: only if you want blog posts, case studies, or richer content pages.
- `dependency-cruiser`: useful later if you want to enforce boundaries between `app`, `components`, `lib`, and admin/public areas.
- `Vercel OG`: strong fit if you want dynamic Open Graph images.

## Curated Report

- `CSpell`: `Use now`. Low-cost quality boost for UI copy, docs, and code spelling.

- `GitHub Actions`: `Use`. Same verdict as above; very relevant for this repo.
- `Mock Service Worker`: `Use soon`. Best companion to `Vitest` and `Playwright` for realistic API mocking.

- `Node.js`: `Keep`. Core runtime for Next, tooling, and CI.

Yes. A few important `Next.js 16`-relevant tools were missing from your list.

## Most Useful Missing Tools
- `@next/bundle-analyzer`
  Best missing tool for your repo. It helps you inspect client/server bundles and is very useful in a portfolio site where bundle size matters.

- `@vercel/analytics`
  Good if you deploy on Vercel and want lightweight traffic/event analytics without adding a heavier analytics stack.

- `@vercel/speed-insights`
  Very relevant for `Next.js` because it gives real Core Web Vitals and route performance data in production.

- `zod`
  This is the big one. For a `Next.js` app with forms, server actions, auth, and DB writes, `zod` is one of the most useful missing tools on the whole list.

- `next-safe-action`
  Strong fit if you lean on Server Actions. It adds typed input validation, safer execution, and cleaner action patterns on top of native Next actions.

- `react-scan`
  Very useful in development to catch unnecessary re-renders and React performance issues, especially in interactive dashboard/admin UI.

- `@axe-core/playwright`
  Excellent if you keep `Playwright`. It gives automated accessibility checks inside E2E tests and fits your public site well.

## Good Missing Tools, But More Optional
- `@vercel/og`
  You listed `Vercel OG`, which is good. If you meant the actual package/tooling layer, this is still worth calling out as a real implementation choice for dynamic OG images.

- `@next/mdx`
  You listed `MDX` and `Next.js MDX`, but the official integration package itself is worth explicitly knowing because that is what you would actually wire into the app.

- `react-hook-form`
  Not mandatory in React 19 + Server Actions, but still very useful if your admin dashboard gets larger, more dynamic forms.

- `axe-core` / `jest-axe` / `vitest-axe`
  Good companions if you want accessibility checks at unit/integration level, not only in browser E2E.

## Things I Would Not Add Despite Being Popular
- `next-seo`
  I would not treat this as a missing tool. In App Router, Next’s native metadata API already covers most SEO work better.

- `Prettier` if you move to `Biome`

- `TanStack Query`
  Only add it if you have a lot of client-side async state, optimistic updates, or repeated client fetching. For a server-first `Next.js 16` app, it is not automatically needed.

3. `@vercel/speed-insights`
4. `@vercel/analytics`
5. `next-safe-action`
6. `@axe-core/playwright`
7. `react-scan`

  --cache-location         Change cache location (default: node_modules/.cache/knip)
  --include-entry-exports  Include entry files when reporting unused exports
  --no-gitignore           Don't respect .gitignore
  --production             Analyze only production source files (e.g. no test files, devDependencies)
  --strict                 Consider only direct dependencies of workspace (not devDependencies, not other workspaces)
  --watch                  Watch mode

Scope
  -W, --workspace [filter] Filter workspaces by name, directory, or glob (can be repeated)
  --directory [dir]        Run process from a different directory (default: cwd)
  --include                Report only provided issue type(s), can be comma-separated or repeated (1)
  --exclude                Exclude provided issue type(s) from report, can be comma-separated or repeated (1)
  --dependencies           Shortcut for --include dependencies,unlisted,binaries,unresolved,catalog
  --exports                Shortcut for --include exports,nsExports,types,nsTypes,enumMembers,namespaceMembers,duplicates
  --files                  Shortcut for --include files
  --tags                   Include or exclude tagged exports

Fix
  --fix                    Fix issues (modifies files in your repo)
  --fix-type               Fix only issues of type, can be comma-separated or repeated (2)
  --allow-remove-files     Allow Knip to remove files (with --fix)
  --format                 Format modified files after --fix using the local formatter

Output
  --preprocessor           Preprocess the results before providing it to the reporter(s), can be repeated
  --preprocessor-options   Pass extra options to the preprocessor (as JSON string, see --reporter-options example)
  --reporter               Select reporter (default: symbols), can be repeated (3)
  --reporter-options       Pass extra options to the reporter (as JSON string, see example)
  --no-config-hints        Suppress configuration hints
  --treat-config-hints-as-errors    Exit with non-zero code (1) if there are any configuration hints
  --max-issues             Maximum number of total issues before non-zero exit code (default: 0)
  --max-show-issues        Maximum number of issues to display per type
  --no-exit-code           Always exit with code zero (0)

Troubleshooting
  -d, --debug              Show debug output
  --memory                 Measure memory usage and display data table
  --memory-realtime        Log memory usage in realtime
  --performance            Measure count and running time of key functions and display stats table
  --performance-fn [name]  Measure only function [name]
  --trace                  Show trace output
  --trace-dependency [name] Show files that import the named dependency
  --trace-export [name]    Show trace output for named export(s)
  --trace-file [file]      Show trace output for exports in file

(1) Issue types: files, dependencies, unlisted, unresolved, exports, nsExports, types, nsTypes, enumMembers, namespaceMembers, duplicates, catalog
(2) Fixable issue types: dependencies, exports, types, files, catalog
(3) Built-in reporters: symbols (default), compact, codeowners, json, codeclimate, markdown, disclosure, github-actions

Examples:

$ knip
$ knip --production
$ knip --workspace packages/client --include files,dependencies
$ knip --workspace @myorg/* --workspace '!@myorg/legacy'
$ knip --workspace './apps/*' --workspace '@shared/utils'
$ knip -c ./config/knip.json --reporter compact
$ knip --reporter codeowners --reporter-options '{"path":".github/CODEOWNERS"}'
$ knip --tags=-lintignore

Website: https://knip.dev

So ideally, these files are included when linting the project. That’s why Knip supports compilers.\n\n## Built-in compilers\n\nKnip has built-in “compilers” for the following file extensions:\n\n- &#96;.astro&#96;\n- &#96;.css&#96;(only enabled by&#96;tailwindcss&#96;)\n- &#96;.mdx&#96;\n- &#96;.prisma&#96;\n- &#96;.sass&#96;+&#96;.scss&#96;\n- &#96;.svelte&#96;\n- &#96;.vue&#96;\n\nKnip does not include real compilers for those files, but regular expressions to collect&#96;import&#96; statements. _**User**_

Why .jsonc instead of .json?

---

_**Agent (composer-2-fast)**_

**`.jsonc`** is JSON **with comments** (and usually trailing commas). **`json`** is plain JSON: no `//` or `/* */` comments.

For this project we used `.jsonc` because the Knip config includes **inline explanations** (why `entry`, `drizzle`, and each `ignoreIssues` glob exist). That same file would be **invalid** as `.json` unless we stripped every comment.

Knip supports both: see [Configuration](https://knip.dev/overview/configuration) — you can use `knip.json` or `knip.jsonc`, and the docs give a separate schema for JSONC (`schema-jsonc.json`).

**When to use which**

| Format | Use when |
|--------|----------|
| **`knip.json`** | No comments; strict JSON only; some tools prefer it. |
| **`knip.jsonc`** | You want comments (and often trailing commas) for maintainability. |

Functionally, Knip treats them the same once parsed. If you prefer strict JSON, rename to `knip.json`, remove the comments, use `$schema` from the non-JSONC schema, and keep the same keys/values.
